dataset.title: Music-based real-time fMRI Neurofeedback
dataset.type: Neuroimaging data from functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging.

dmp.description: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has created new ways for neuroscientists to explore the intricate functioning of the human brain. By reading and analyzing fMRI data in real-time, i.e., as it is being acquired, a new type of intervention has emerged - real-time fMRI neurofeedback - a loop system in which the feedback stimuli are adapted to the participant’s measured brain activity as it fires. This feedback information has usually been provided to the participant in some form of visual cue. The project presented here aims to test the feasibility of using music to convey the feedback message, that is, to act as the interface of the neurofeedback system. The relationship between music and the human brain is a topic of significant importance in cognitive neuroscience. Its perception involves a number of different mechanisms, namely to interpret rhythm, harmony, and melody, which were found to map into distinct regions of the brain. What has intrigued scientists for many years is that music, just like language, has existed in all human societies as a complex but organized feature that develops early in life. Although the evolutionary function of music remains unknown, studies have suggested its ability to engage essential brain networks - music seems especially proficient in triggering emotional processes and engaging the brain’s limbic and reward circuits. This project is divided into three stages: we start by optimizing the MRI sequence to be used, calculating quality measures relevant for the application; then, we try to reduce one of the most commonly reported discomforts of the MRI scanner - the noise - by developing a simple, open-source solution, for active noise canceling; finally, we will merge these technical advances to design a neurofeedback experiment which uses music as the interface between the participant and its own brain activity. If successful, this project will create the foundation for a rehabilitation procedure/intervention that combines one of the most advanced neuroimaging techniques with an arguably universal language - music - to be used in a wide range of applications.
